words.shortDefinition: A GCE instance that encrypts the contents of RAM using AMD SEV hardware, protecting in-use data from the hypervisor and Google's own infrastructure staff.
words.simpleDefinition: A Confidential VM encrypts the VM's memory in hardware using AMD Secure Encrypted Virtualization (SEV). Even if Google's hypervisor, a rogue employee, or a compromised host is able to read raw memory, they see only encrypted data — the decryption key exists only inside the CPU and is never accessible to the host OS or hypervisor.
words.longDefinition: Confidential Computing addresses a gap in cloud security: data at rest (disk encryption) and data in transit (TLS) have been solved, but data in use — sitting in RAM during computation — is traditionally accessible to the cloud provider's hypervisor. Confidential VMs use AMD Secure Encrypted Virtualization (SEV or SEV-SNP on newer hardware) to encrypt guest VM memory with a key that is generated inside the AMD Secure Processor and never exposed to the hypervisor or host kernel. Key properties: (1) Memory encryption — all DRAM is encrypted with a VM-specific key derived inside the CPU; (2) Attestation — the AMD SEV firmware generates a cryptographically signed attestation report that proves which guest image and which CPU firmware version is running, allowing the workload owner to verify the trusted execution environment (TEE) before sending sensitive data; (3) Confidential GKE Nodes — extends memory encryption to GKE worker nodes so pods run in an encrypted memory context. Confidential VMs run on N2D (AMD EPYC) machine types. Performance overhead is approximately 0–6% for most workloads. Use cases: processing healthcare PHI or financial data where the cloud provider must be kept in the trusted computing base exclusion, secure multi-party computation where parties share compute but not raw data, and regulatory requirements (GDPR, HIPAA) that demand end-to-end confidentiality including in-use data.
words.connector: Think of a Confidential VM like doing sensitive paperwork inside a bank vault — even the bank employees who own the building cannot read what you're writing because the vault's walls are made of encryption rather than steel.
words.techContext: Our genomics pipeline processes patient sequencing data on Confidential VMs — the SEV attestation report lets our compliance team verify that the data is processed inside a trusted execution environment where even Google's infrastructure cannot access the plaintext reads.
words.exampleSentence: Switching to Confidential VMs for our PII processing workload satisfied the data processing agreement with our European partner, which required that the cloud provider be cryptographically excluded from access to data in use.

codeExample.code:
# Create a Confidential VM (requires N2D machine type + AMD EPYC)
gcloud compute instances create confidential-worker \
  --zone=us-central1-a \
  --machine-type=n2d-standard-8 \
  --image-family=ubuntu-2204-lts \
  --image-project=ubuntu-os-cloud \
  --confidential-compute \
  --shielded-secure-boot

words.etymology: Confidential from Latin confidere ('to trust fully'), meaning data shared only with authorized parties; Confidential Computing as a term was popularized by the Confidential Computing Consortium (CCC), a Linux Foundation project founded in 2019.

words.shortDefinition: A Cloud KMS backend that stores cryptographic keys inside FIPS 140-2 Level 3 certified hardware security modules, ensuring keys can never be exported in plaintext.
words.simpleDefinition: Cloud HSM is an option within Cloud KMS that stores your encryption keys in a physical Hardware Security Module — a tamper-resistant chip that is FIPS 140-2 Level 3 certified. Unlike software-based KMS keys, an HSM key's raw material never exists outside the dedicated hardware, satisfying the strictest key custody requirements.
words.longDefinition: Cloud HSM extends Cloud KMS by offering an HSM-backed key protection level. While standard Cloud KMS keys are protected by Google's software key management infrastructure (itself highly secure), some compliance frameworks — PCI DSS, FedRAMP High, certain financial regulations — require that cryptographic keys be stored in a FIPS 140-2 Level 3 validated hardware security module where physical tamper response mechanisms destroy keys if the device is opened. Cloud HSM uses Google-operated HSM clusters (currently Marvell/Cavium LiquidSecurity) deployed in Google's datacenters. From a developer perspective, Cloud HSM keys are used identically to standard Cloud KMS keys — same API, same IAM, same audit logging. The key's protection level (`HSM`) is specified at creation time and cannot be changed afterward. HSM-backed keys support the same operations as software keys: AES-256-GCM encryption, RSA signing (2048/3072/4096), EC signing (P-256, P-384), and key import (wrapping with an RSA key generated inside the HSM). The performance difference is minimal for signing and decryption at normal call rates. Cloud HSM is the right choice when the compliance requirement is specifically about hardware protection of the root of trust, as opposed to operational security of key access (which Cloud KMS addresses equally well).
words.connector: Think of Cloud HSM like keeping the master key to your safe in a bank safe-deposit box rather than in a home safe — the bank's vault has physical tamper-evident protections and independent certifications that go beyond what a home safe can offer.
words.techContext: Our PCI DSS Level 1 certification required FIPS 140-2 Level 3 key protection for cardholder data encryption — we migrated from standard Cloud KMS to Cloud HSM-backed keys during our QSA audit, and the change was entirely transparent to our application code since both use the same KMS API.
words.exampleSentence: Cloud HSM gave us the FIPS 140-2 Level 3 certification evidence our auditors required without deploying any on-premises HSM appliances — we got hardware-grade key protection as a managed service with the same Cloud KMS API our applications already used.

codeExample.code:
# Create an HSM-backed key in Cloud KMS
gcloud kms keyrings create hsm-ring \
  --location=us-central1

gcloud kms keys create payment-enc-key \
  --keyring=hsm-ring \
  --location=us-central1 \
  --purpose=encryption \
  --protection-level=hsm

# Verify protection level
gcloud kms keys describe payment-enc-key \
  --keyring=hsm-ring \
  --location=us-central1 \
  --format='value(primary.protectionLevel)'
# Output: HSM

words.etymology: HSM stands for Hardware Security Module — a physical device for safeguarding and managing cryptographic keys; the term dates to the 1980s in financial computing; Cloud HSM is Google's managed offering, integrating physical HSM hardware into the Cloud KMS service.

words.shortDefinition: A GCP service that enforces identity and device-level access policies at the application layer, enabling zero-trust access to internal apps without a VPN.
words.simpleDefinition: Identity-Aware Proxy (IAP) sits in front of your web apps and cloud VMs and enforces Google identity authentication before any request reaches your application. Users authenticate with their Google or Workspace account, and IAP checks their group membership and device posture before forwarding the request — making your internal app accessible over the internet without a VPN.
words.longDefinition: Identity-Aware Proxy implements the BeyondCorp zero-trust model at the application access layer. Traditional network-perimeter security grants access to all applications once a user is on the corporate VPN. IAP moves the control to the individual application level: each app protected by IAP requires a separate authentication and authorization check based on the user's Google identity, their IAM role, and optionally their device's trust level (managed, verified). IAP intercepts every HTTP/HTTPS request at the Cloud Load Balancer, validates the user's Google identity token, checks their IAM `roles/iap.httpsResourceAccessor` binding on the specific resource, and either forwards the request (with injected `X-Goog-Authenticated-User-Email` and `X-Goog-IAP-JWT-Assertion` headers) or returns a 403. For SSH/RDP access to GCE VMs, IAP TCP tunneling creates an encrypted tunnel through IAP without requiring the VM to have a public IP address. IAP also integrates with Cloud Armor for DDoS protection and Access Context Manager for device posture conditions (require managed device enrollment, require specific OS patch level). The result is a globally accessible, identity-verified entry point to internal applications — employees access internal tools from any location, on any network, without a VPN client.
words.connector: Think of Identity-Aware Proxy like a very sophisticated bouncer at every door in a building — instead of checking your badge once at the front lobby (VPN), the bouncer personally verifies your identity and clearance before letting you into each individual room.
words.techContext: We replaced our corporate VPN for developer tool access by placing all internal services behind IAP with device trust policies — developers access our internal dashboards from home networks using their Workspace credentials, and IAP ensures only managed laptops with current patches are admitted.
words.exampleSentence: Identity-Aware Proxy let our remote-first team access internal engineering tools over the internet without distributing VPN clients — IAP enforces Workspace authentication and checks that the user's device is enrolled in our MDM before allowing any connection.

codeExample.code:
# Enable IAP on a Cloud Run service via load balancer backend
gcloud iap web enable \
  --resource-type=backend-services \
  --service=my-internal-app-backend

# Grant a user access through IAP
gcloud iap web add-iam-policy-binding \
  --resource-type=backend-services \
  --service=my-internal-app-backend \
  --member='user:alice@example.com' \
  --role='roles/iap.httpsResourceAccessor'

# IAP TCP tunnel to a VM without public IP
gcloud compute start-iap-tunnel my-vm 22 \
  --local-host-port=localhost:2222 \
  --zone=us-central1-a

words.etymology: Identity-Aware from the BeyondCorp security model where authorization depends on the user's verified identity rather than network location; Proxy because IAP intercepts and mediates all requests; the concept was introduced by Google BeyondCorp paper (2014) and productized as Cloud IAP in 2017.

words.shortDefinition: Google's zero-trust access platform for enterprises, combining IAP, endpoint verification, and threat intelligence into a comprehensive VPN-replacement solution.
words.simpleDefinition: BeyondCorp Enterprise is Google's full-featured zero-trust access product. It bundles Identity-Aware Proxy with endpoint certificate verification, Chrome Enterprise device trust signals, DLP controls, and threat intelligence — replacing the corporate VPN with a model where user identity and device health are verified on every request, not just at network entry.
words.longDefinition: BeyondCorp Enterprise is the commercialization of Google's internal BeyondCorp program — the zero-trust architecture Google built after the 2009 Aurora cyberattack convinced leadership that the traditional VPN + trusted-corporate-network model was fundamentally broken. The core insight: VPN grants network-level trust to a device once connected; BeyondCorp grants application-level access based on real-time evaluation of user identity, device state, and request context on every request. BeyondCorp Enterprise integrates multiple capabilities: (1) Identity-Aware Proxy (IAP) for application-layer access control; (2) Endpoint Verification — a Chrome extension or Endpoint Verification agent that reports device attributes (OS version, disk encryption status, MDM enrollment, screen lock) as trust signals; (3) Access Context Manager — defines access levels based on device policy (`requireCorpOwned`, `requireEncryption`) and network attributes; (4) Chrome Enterprise Premium — the browser becomes the secure access layer, enforcing DLP policies (blocking copy-paste of sensitive data to unmanaged destinations), screenshot prevention, and watermarking; (5) Threat and Data Protection — integration with Cloud Armor and reCAPTCHA for bot/DDoS defense, and Cloud DLP for real-time data inspection. For SaaS apps and Google Workspace, BeyondCorp integrates through SAML and OIDC federation. The result is a security model where network access is irrelevant — a user on an unmanaged coffee shop WiFi with a fully managed, up-to-date corporate laptop gets exactly the same access as a user on the corporate LAN, because access decisions are based on identity and device posture, not network topology.
words.connector: Think of BeyondCorp Enterprise like a building where every door has a biometric scanner and a health check — you don't get a master key badge when you enter the lobby; instead, every door verifies who you are and whether you're cleared for that specific room, every single time.
words.techContext: We implemented BeyondCorp Enterprise with endpoint verification to eliminate split-tunnel VPN for our 2,000-person engineering org — Access Context Manager policies now ensure that only corporate-managed devices with FileVault enabled can access production internal tools, regardless of network location.
words.exampleSentence: BeyondCorp Enterprise's device trust signals let us retire our always-on VPN — when a developer's laptop falls below the required OS patch level, Access Context Manager automatically downgrades their access to read-only until they update, without any manual helpdesk intervention.
words.etymology: BeyondCorp is a play on 'beyond the corporate perimeter' — the philosophical departure from the trusted-network model; Enterprise indicates the enterprise product tier; the name references Google's internal security program described in a series of USENIX ;login: papers starting in 2014.

words.shortDefinition: GCP's centralized security management and threat intelligence platform that continuously monitors GCP assets for vulnerabilities, misconfigurations, and active threats.
words.simpleDefinition: Security Command Center (SCC) is GCP's built-in security posture platform. It automatically scans all your GCP resources for vulnerabilities and misconfigurations — public GCS buckets, open firewall rules, IAM over-permissions — and surfaces active threats like cryptomining attacks or data exfiltration attempts, all in a single dashboard.
words.longDefinition: Security Command Center is Google Cloud's centralized security intelligence platform, analogous to AWS Security Hub or Azure Defender for Cloud. It aggregates findings from multiple Google-native security services and third-party integrations into a single console. Built-in finding sources: (1) Security Health Analytics — continuously scans GCP configuration for common misconfigurations (publicly readable GCS buckets, default service accounts with Editor role, VMs with no OS Login, Firestore public access); (2) Web Security Scanner — crawls Cloud Run and App Engine web applications for XSS, mixed content, and other OWASP vulnerabilities; (3) Container Threat Detection — detects suspicious processes inside GKE containers (reverse shells, crypto miners, privilege escalation attempts) using low-level OS telemetry; (4) Event Threat Detection — correlates Cloud Logging events to detect account takeover, data exfiltration, and privilege abuse patterns using Google Threat Intelligence data; (5) Virtual Machine Threat Detection — detects malicious code running inside GCE VMs by analyzing memory from the hypervisor level without installing an agent. SCC Premium tier adds attack path simulation (showing how an attacker could move from a vulnerability to sensitive data), compliance dashboards (CIS benchmarks, PCI DSS, NIST 800-53), and posture management for Kubernetes and BigQuery. Findings export to Chronicle (Google's SIEM), Cloud Logging, or Pub/Sub for SIEM integration.
words.connector: Think of Security Command Center like a security operations center (SOC) built into your GCP account — instead of hiring a team to manually check every resource configuration, SCC continuously scans everything and alerts on deviations, misconfigurations, and active threats.
words.techContext: Security Command Center Premium's attack path simulation showed us that a misconfigured Compute Engine service account binding created a 4-step privilege escalation path from a compromised VM to our Cloud Spanner production database — we patched the finding in 20 minutes before any attacker could exploit it.
words.exampleSentence: Security Command Center's Event Threat Detection fired within 8 minutes of a compromised service account starting to enumerate Cloud Storage buckets — the finding linked directly to the specific audit log entries so our security team could immediately revoke the credential and assess the blast radius.

# List active SCC findings of HIGH severity
gcloud scc findings list organizations/123456789 \
  --filter='state=ACTIVE AND severity=HIGH' \
  --format='table(name, category, resourceName, createTime)'

# Export findings to BigQuery for trend analysis
gcloud scc findings list organizations/123456789 \
  --format=json \
  | bq insert my-project:security.scc_findings -

words.etymology: Security Command Center name draws from military Command and Control centers (C2) — a centralized command post with visibility across the entire theater of operations; Google Cloud introduced the product in 2018.

words.shortDefinition: A GCP distributed tracing service that collects latency data across microservices, surfaces high-latency request spans, and helps identify performance bottlenecks.
words.simpleDefinition: Cloud Trace collects distributed tracing data from your GCP services — each request generates a trace composed of spans across all services it touches. Cloud Trace stores these traces, analyzes them to identify slow operations, and surfaces latency distributions so you can pinpoint which service or database query is responsible for p99 slowness.
words.longDefinition: Cloud Trace is Google Cloud's managed distributed tracing backend, compatible with OpenTelemetry, Zipkin, and the Cloud Trace API directly. When a request enters your system, a trace context (trace ID, span ID) is propagated through every downstream service call via HTTP headers (`X-Cloud-Trace-Context` or W3C Trace-Context). Each service creates a span — a named, timed operation — and reports it to Cloud Trace. The trace backend assembles these spans into a timeline showing the full latency contribution of every component. Key capabilities: (1) Latency distribution analysis — Cloud Trace aggregates all traces for a given URL/RPC and shows p50, p95, p99 latency over time; (2) Trace comparison — compare traces from before and after a code change to identify regressions; (3) Integration with Cloud Profiler and Cloud Logging — traces link directly to the log entries and CPU profiles recorded during the same request, enabling drill-down from a slow trace to the specific function consuming CPU; (4) Auto-instrumentation — GKE Autopilot and Cloud Run automatically inject basic trace context for HTTP requests; you add custom spans for database queries and background operations. Cloud Trace is priced per trace ingested and is often the first tool a team reaches for when p99 latency mysteriously increases after a deployment.
words.connector: Think of Cloud Trace like a package tracking system for API requests — every request gets a tracking number and every service it passes through stamps its arrival and departure time, so you can see exactly where the delay occurred on the journey.
words.techContext: Cloud Trace revealed that our checkout API's p99 latency spike was caused by a single Spanner read that had exploded from 12ms to 340ms after a schema migration — the trace showed the exact query plan and we added the missing secondary index to fix it.
words.exampleSentence: Cloud Trace showed that 95% of our API's tail latency came from a single database query that only became slow when the request included more than 20 items — a finding we would never have identified by looking at average query times alone.

codeExample.code:
from opentelemetry import trace
from opentelemetry.exporter.cloud_trace import CloudTraceSpanExporter
from opentelemetry.sdk.trace import TracerProvider
from opentelemetry.sdk.trace.export import BatchSpanProcessor

# Configure OpenTelemetry to export to Cloud Trace
tracer_provider = TracerProvider()
tracer_provider.add_span_processor(
    BatchSpanProcessor(CloudTraceSpanExporter())
)
trace.set_tracer_provider(tracer_provider)

tracer = trace.get_tracer(__name__)

def process_order(order_id):
    with tracer.start_as_current_span('process_order') as span:
        span.set_attribute('order.id', order_id)
        result = db.query_order(order_id)  # sub-span auto-created if instrumented
        return result

words.etymology: Trace from Latin trahere ('to draw/track'); Cloud Trace was originally Stackdriver Trace, rebranded as part of the Cloud Operations Suite in 2020; the distributed tracing concept originates from Google's Dapper paper (2010).

words.shortDefinition: A GCP continuous CPU and memory profiling service that collects statistical call-stack data from production workloads with negligible overhead.
words.simpleDefinition: Cloud Profiler runs continuously in your production services, sampling call stacks a few hundred times per second to build a statistical picture of where CPU time is spent. It presents this as a flame graph showing which functions are hot across your entire fleet over time — finding performance regressions without requiring a load test or special profiling run.
words.longDefinition: Cloud Profiler is a statistical production profiling service inspired by Google's internal Borg profiler, which continuously profiles the entire production fleet. It uses low-overhead sampling profiling (statistical, not deterministic) — the profiling agent interrupts execution a few hundred times per second, records the current call stack, and sends aggregated samples to Cloud Profiler backend. The overhead is typically under 1% CPU. Supported profile types: CPU time (wall-clock time on CPU), CPU time (time scheduled on CPU, including contention), heap (memory allocated and retained), heap allocation (allocation rate), threads (concurrent goroutine/thread counts). Languages supported: Go, Java, Node.js, Python, Ruby, and any language through the OpenTelemetry profiling API. The Cloud Profiler UI presents profiles as a flame graph (aggregated across all instances in the fleet) and allows comparison between time ranges — deploy a new version and immediately compare the CPU profile before and after to detect regressions. Cloud Profiler integrates with Cloud Trace and Cloud Logging: if you have an active trace, Cloud Profiler shows the profile collected during that specific trace's time window. Unlike one-shot local profiling, Cloud Profiler's continuous data means you can investigate a performance issue that happened yesterday by examining historical profiles, even if you weren't actively profiling at the time.
words.connector: Think of Cloud Profiler like a fitness tracker for your code — it continuously monitors how your functions are spending their time throughout the day, and you can review the data whenever you suspect something is consuming more energy than it should.
words.techContext: Cloud Profiler's flame graph comparison revealed that after deploying a new version of our gRPC service, the JSON serialization library was consuming 18% of CPU — up from 3% in the previous version — because a developer accidentally changed from streaming serialization to loading entire responses into memory.
words.exampleSentence: Cloud Profiler showed that 30% of CPU time in our Go microservice was spent in GC due to a hot allocation loop — the flame graph clearly pointed to a specific loop creating thousands of short-lived byte slices per request, which we fixed with a sync.Pool.
words.etymology: Profiler from Latin profilare ('to outline'); the concept of statistical sampling profilers dates to gprof (1982); Cloud Profiler was originally Stackdriver Profiler, rebranded in 2020, and is the productized version of Google's internal continuous profiling infrastructure.

words.shortDefinition: A managed Istio-based service mesh for GKE that provides mTLS encryption, traffic management, and distributed observability across microservices.
words.simpleDefinition: Anthos Service Mesh (ASM) is Google's managed Istio distribution for GKE. It injects a sidecar proxy into every pod to handle mTLS encryption, traffic splitting for canary deployments, automatic distributed tracing, and rich golden-signal dashboards — without changing any application code.
words.longDefinition: Anthos Service Mesh is a Google-managed version of Istio, the open-source service mesh. A service mesh adds a layer of infrastructure-level networking capabilities to Kubernetes without application code changes: each pod gets a sidecar Envoy proxy injected automatically, which intercepts all inbound and outbound traffic. ASM capabilities: (1) mTLS between all services — certificates are provisioned and rotated automatically by the mesh's certificate authority (Mesh CA or Google Certificate Authority Service); (2) Traffic management — fine-grained routing rules (header-based routing, percentage-based traffic splits for canary deployments, retries, circuit breaking) configured via Istio VirtualService and DestinationRule objects; (3) Observability — all traffic metrics (request rate, error rate, latency) are automatically emitted to Cloud Monitoring for golden-signal dashboards without any application instrumentation; distributed tracing headers are injected and reported to Cloud Trace; (4) Authorization policies — mesh-level mTLS policies enforce that only specific services can talk to each other, providing defense-in-depth beyond Kubernetes NetworkPolicies. ASM Managed mode (the recommended configuration) eliminates istiod management — Google upgrades the control plane, patches CVEs, and maintains compatibility with GKE releases. ASM integrates with GKE Autopilot and multi-cluster GKE environments, extending mTLS and observability across clusters in different regions.
words.connector: Think of Anthos Service Mesh like replacing all the informal phone calls between departments with a professional switchboard that records every call, encrypts every line, and can redirect a call mid-conversation based on any rule you define — without asking each department to change their phone.
words.techContext: After enabling Anthos Service Mesh, our platform team got automatic golden-signal dashboards for every microservice — request rate, error rate, and p99 latency per service pair — without any application-side instrumentation work, which would have taken months across 60 services.
words.exampleSentence: Anthos Service Mesh's automatic mTLS enforcement caught a misconfigured service that was accepting unencrypted traffic — the mesh's telemetry showed clear-text connections from one legacy service that had missed the mTLS migration, something our manual audit had not detected.

codeExample.code:
# ASM traffic split: canary 10% of traffic to v2
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: VirtualService
metadata:
  name: checkout
spec:
  hosts: [checkout]
  http:
    - route:
        - destination:
            host: checkout
            subset: v1
          weight: 90
        - destination:
            host: checkout
            subset: v2
          weight: 10
---
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: DestinationRule
metadata:
  name: checkout
spec:
  host: checkout
  subsets:
    - name: v1
      labels: {version: v1}
    - name: v2
      labels: {version: v2}

words.etymology: Anthos from Greek anthos ('flower') — Google's multi-cloud platform brand; Service Mesh from the network topology metaphor where services are interconnected nodes in a mesh; Istio (the underlying technology) from Greek ιστίο ('sail').

words.shortDefinition: A GKE add-on that continuously syncs Kubernetes configuration from a Git repository to one or more clusters, implementing the GitOps pattern as a managed service.
words.simpleDefinition: Config Sync is Google's managed GitOps controller for GKE. It continuously watches a Git repository containing Kubernetes manifests and applies any changes to your clusters automatically — ensuring that cluster state always matches the declared configuration in Git, and alerting when drift is detected. It is Flux or Argo CD, but managed by Google.
words.longDefinition: Config Sync is part of the Anthos Config Management product and implements the GitOps continuous reconciliation pattern as a managed GKE add-on. You configure Config Sync with a pointer to a Git repository (or an OCI image registry containing Kubernetes manifests) and it runs a controller in each enrolled cluster that continuously polls the source and applies any delta configuration. Key capabilities: (1) Multi-cluster sync — one config repo can govern configurations across dozens of clusters (multi-region, multi-tenant GKE) from a single source of truth; (2) Hierarchical configuration — the RepoSync and RootSync CRDs allow different configuration scopes per namespace or cluster, enabling platform teams to govern cluster-level resources while application teams manage namespace-level configs; (3) Drift detection and auto-remediation — if a user manually edits a resource managed by Config Sync, the controller detects the drift and reconciles back to the Git state within seconds; (4) Policy Controller integration — Config Sync works alongside Policy Controller (OPA Gatekeeper) so that only policy-compliant resources are applied; (5) Audit logging — every sync operation is recorded in Cloud Logging with the commit SHA and author, providing a complete audit trail of every configuration change deployed. Config Sync eliminates manual `kubectl apply` operations in production — cluster state changes only by merging a PR, which is reviewed, tested in a staging cluster, and auto-applied. This is the GitOps principle applied to the full GKE operational model.
words.connector: Think of Config Sync like a document synchronization service for your Kubernetes clusters — whatever you write in the Git 'document' (the manifest repo) automatically appears in the cluster, and if someone scribbles on the cluster directly, Config Sync erases it and restores the Git version.
words.techContext: Config Sync syncs our platform team's cluster configuration repo to 12 regional GKE clusters simultaneously — when we merge a NetworkPolicy PR, it is applied to all clusters within 30 seconds, and any drift introduced by an emergency `kubectl` is auto-remediated from the audit log within minutes.
words.exampleSentence: Config Sync's drift detection caught an emergency NetworkPolicy change that a SRE had applied directly to production during an incident — the tool flagged the out-of-band change in Cloud Logging within 60 seconds, and we captured it in a PR before the next reconciliation reverted it.

codeExample.code:
# Config Sync RootSync configuration (applied to the cluster once)
apiVersion: configsync.gke.io/v1beta1
kind: RootSync
metadata:
  name: root-sync
  namespace: config-management-system
spec:
  sourceFormat: hierarchy
  git:
    repo: https://github.com/myorg/gke-platform-config
    branch: main
    dir: clusters/prod-us-central1
    auth: gcpserviceaccount
    gcpServiceAccountEmail: config-sync-sa@my-project.iam.gserviceaccount.com
  override:
    reconcileTimeout: 5m

words.etymology: Config short for Configuration; Sync short for Synchronization — the continuous process of keeping cluster state aligned with the declared state in Git; Config Sync is part of Google's Anthos Config Management product, generally available since 2021.
